title: Data Science with R for Environmental, Agricultural, and Social Scientists
text: Course materials for Data Science with R (AECN 896-05) at UNL, redesigned for working alongside AI. The lectures teach what each step of a data project is, what has to be true for it to succeed, what to ask an AI assistant to do, and how to check what comes back.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the files contain, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 1: Look and predict
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 162 lines: one line of column names and 161 data rows.
B. 9 columns: Year, State, FIPS, County_name, State_name, Commodity, Data item, Irrigated, Yield. County_name, State_name, Commodity and Data item are text; the rest are numbers. Data item has a space in its name.
C. One county, one year, and one irrigation status (Irrigated is 0 or 1), so most counties appear twice.
D. Two sheets, corn_yields_08 and corn_yields_09.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 2: Read the csv
text:
Task 2: Read the csv






What you should find





161 rows and 9 columns, no missing values, and yields from 103 to 204 bushels per acre.
The checks, and why. The five from the lecture, each tied to a way this import could go wrong:

Rows and columns: a title line read as data, or the reader stopping early, changes the count from the 161 you counted.
Type of every column: Yield read as text would make every later calculation fail or mislead.
Missing values per column: a column that failed to read shows up as all missing.
Range of Yield: a code such as -999, or a number in the wrong units, shows up as an impossible value.
The first row: shifted columns show up when compared with the first data line of the file.

The blanks of the recommended request, filled in:
- above the column names there is nothing
- there are 161 data rows and 9 columns
- one row is one county, one year, and one irrigation status
- missing values are written as: none expected
- ID columns that must stay text: FIPS
- a believable range for Yield is 100 to 250
In the HTML, every “expected, got” line should match.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Both sheets of the Excel file
text:
Task 3: Both sheets of the Excel file






What you should find





161 + 161 = 322 rows. Year is 2008 in one sheet and 2009 in the other.
The check from knowing the data. Yields change from year to year, because the weather does, so each county’s yield should differ between the two years. Asking “is each county’s yield the same in both years?” gives TRUE: every county has exactly the same yield.
That cannot be real data. The code is fine; the file is wrong, and no change to the code fixes it. The right move is to stop and ask whoever produced the file, and not to analyse year-to-year changes until you have an answer.
This is the point of the task: the row count and the types all passed. Only a check you thought of, because you know something about corn, caught the problem.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 4: A messy file
text:
Task 4: A messy file






What you should find





4a, the short request. Plain read_csv() treats the first description line as the column names, so you get 94 rows and only 3 columns with sentence fragments for names, plus a warning about parsing problems. Base R’s read.csv() stops with an error instead. Either way the problem is visible, which is the good case.
4b, the file. Two lines of description sit above the column names. Missing yields are written two ways, -999 and ., and the second description line says so. county_fips holds 5-digit county codes, and the 5 Colorado codes start with 08. There are 95 lines, so 92 data rows.
4c, a correct result. 92 rows, 5 columns, county_fips is text with the leading zeros kept, yield is a number, 5 yields are missing, and the rest run from 102 to 199. Average yield: 157.7.
The checks, and the problem each one catches in this file:

Rows: the description lines read as data.
Type of county_fips: the leading 0 of the Colorado codes lost.
Type of the yield column: text instead of a number, because of the . entries.
Number of missing yields: should be 5. Fewer means a missing-value code was kept as a value.
Range of yields: a minimum of -999 means the -999 code was not recognised.

The silent trap. If your request mentioned . but not -999, the yield column is a number, nothing errors, and the average comes out at 119.2. Checks 4 and 5 both catch it.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Maria’s code
text:
Task 5: Maria’s code






Answers





A. Read the file, skipping the two description lines and treating . as missing; rename the fifth column to yield; average the yields, ignoring missing ones.
B. The path. C:/Users/maria/Downloads exists only on Maria’s computer.
C. First, -999 is not treated as missing, so the average is 119.2 instead of 157.7. Second, read.csv() reads county_fips as a number, so 08125 becomes 8125. Nothing uses that column here, but the first time Maria joins this table to another one by county code, the Colorado counties will quietly fail to match.
D. “Print the smallest and largest yield”: a minimum of -999 is impossible. “Print the type of every column”: county_fips should be text, because it is an ID, not a quantity.
E. The AI usually spots the path and often the -999. It can only spot the -999 because the code itself is visible to it; it has not seen the file. Whether it notices the lost leading zero varies. Either way, compare its list with yours, and treat its answer like any other: something to check, not something to accept.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 6: Save and read back
text:
Task 6: Save and read back






What you should find





The rds file comes back identical. The csv file comes back with state_name as plain text rather than a factor, because a csv stores only text and the reader has to guess types again. This is why the lecture recommends rds for results you will read back into R.
If the AI compares with all.equal(), the csv comparison prints several lines starting with Attributes: before the one that matters, Component "state_name": 'current' is not a factor. The Attributes lines are about hidden bookkeeping that read_csv() attaches to every table it reads, not about your data. Ask the AI which lines are about the data itself if this is unclear.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Does it run anywhere?
text:
Task 7: Does it run anywhere?






What you should find





If it fails on your neighbour’s computer, the error names the line that depended on your machine, almost always a path. Ask the AI to fix that line, explaining what failed, and try again. A worksheet that renders on someone else’s computer unchanged is the final check that every path in it is relative to the project.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can write the code that reads a file into R. It knows every function and every argument. What it cannot do is:

see the files on your computer
know what is inside them
know what the data is for
tell whether the result is right

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what importing and exporting are, and what has to be true for them to work
Reading code: recognising what a line of import code does, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: how to tell whether the code the AI wrote did the right thing




Clone this repository, which holds the datasets used here
Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse and haven packages if you have not already. Installing is a one-time step per computer (see the packages slide in Chapter 1).

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What importing is
text:
What importing is
A data file is a table saved on disk in some format. Importing means a function reads that file and builds a table inside R (a data frame) that you give a name to.
Every import line you will see has the same three parts:

corn <- read_csv("corn_yields.csv")









Part
Here
What it is




Name
corn
What you will call the table inside R. <- stores the result under that name.


Reader
read_csv
The function that understands this file’s format


Path
"corn_yields.csv"
Where the file is



The AI will pick the reader and fill in the details. You need to be able to look at a line like this and say which part is which.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What has to be true for an import to work
text:
What has to be true for an import to work

The four conditionsLoud and silent failures



R can find the file. The path points at a file that exists.
The reader matches the format. A csv reader for a csv file, an Excel reader for an Excel file.
The reader understands the layout. Where the column names are, which sheet to read, what marks a missing value.
Each column gets the right type. Numbers as numbers, text as text, IDs kept exactly as written.




If condition 1 or 2 fails, R stops with an error. Annoying, but you know something is wrong.
If condition 3 or 4 fails, R gives you a data frame with no error, and the data frame is wrong.




Important


The silent failures are why checking matters. Code that runs is not the same as code that is right.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Condition 1: R can find the file
text:
Condition 1: R can find the file

PathsThe project root and here()Why AI gets this wrong


A path is the address of a file. There are two kinds:

Absolute path: starts at the top of the disk, for example "/Users/taro/Documents/class/corn_yields.csv". It works only on the computer it was written on, because nobody else has those folders.
Relative path: starts from the folder R is currently in (the working directory), for example "data/corn_yields.csv". It works on any computer that has the same project folder.

What R treats as the working directory:

At the Console: your project folder (if you opened an R Project)
Inside a .qmd file: the folder the .qmd is saved in



The safest path is one measured from the top of your project folder (the project root). The here package does that. Recognise it when you see it:

corn <- read_csv(here::here("data", "corn_yields.csv"))

This reads data/corn_yields.csv inside your project, whichever subfolder your code is in and whoever’s computer it runs on.


The AI cannot see your folders, so it guesses the path. Its guesses tend to be one of these:

just the file name, assuming the file is in the working directory
an absolute path copied from an example, such as "C:/Users/yourname/..."
setwd(...) to change the working directory first

All three break as soon as the code runs somewhere else. Tell it where the file is (see “Asking AI” below).

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Condition 2: the reader matches the format
text:
Condition 2: the reader matches the format
The file extension (the part after the last dot) tells you the format. You do not need to memorise the reader; tell the AI the extension and it will pick one. You do need to recognise them:









Extension
Format
Reader you will see
What the file remembers




.csv
plain text, any software opens it
read_csv() (readr)
Only text. Types are guessed on reading.


.xls, .xlsx
Excel workbook
read_excel() (readxl)
Several sheets per file


.dta
STATA
read_dta() (haven)
Types and variable labels


.rds
R’s own format
readRDS() (built in)
The exact R object, nothing guessed






Note


A csv file stores everything as text, so the reader has to guess each column’s type. That guessing is where conditions 3 and 4 go wrong.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Conditions 3 and 4: the silent failures
text:
Conditions 3 and 4: the silent failures

Lost leading zerosCodes for missing valuesThe wrong sheet


County codes (FIPS) for Alabama start with 0. Here is a tiny csv, written straight into the code, and what the reader makes of it:

small_csv <- "fips,county,yield
01001,Autauga,150
01003,Baldwin,-999
31019,Buffalo,173"

small <- read_csv(I(small_csv), show_col_types = FALSE)
small$fips

[1] "01001" "01003" "31019"

read.csv(text = small_csv)$fips

[1]  1001  1003 31019


The two readers guessed differently about the same file. read_csv() kept 01001 as text. read.csv(), the built-in reader that AI assistants often write, decided the column was a number and turned 01001 into 1001. No error either way. Later, joining that table to another one by fips would quietly fail to match these counties.


The same file uses -999 to mean “no data”, a common convention. The reader does not know that:

mean(small$yield)

[1] -225.3333


An average yield of -225.3 bushels per acre. Again no error. The reader has to be told that -999 means missing.


corn_yields.xls has two sheets:

readxl::excel_sheets("corn_yields.xls")

[1] "corn_yields_08" "corn_yields_09"


A reader told nothing about sheets reads the first one only. If you wanted both years, you now have half the data, with no error.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: How you work with the AI in this course
text:
How you work with the AI in this course
Every piece of work in this course lives in a Quarto document (.qmd), and you judge it by reading the HTML file it renders to.

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into your .qmd. Code goes into code chunks, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.

Why the HTML and not the chat window:

Rendering runs every chunk from the top in a fresh R session. If the HTML is right, the work is reproducible; nothing depends on something typed into the Console and forgotten.
It puts each explanation, its code and its result in one place, in order.
It is what you hand in, and what anyone else will read.




Note


Every request ends with the same few lines telling the AI to work this way. This deck calls them the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI already knows the functions. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The file: its name, its format, and where it sits inside your project
What is inside: the first few lines, the sheet names, and anything unusual (IDs with leading zeros, codes for missing values)
What you want back: the name of the table, what one row is, and which type each key column should be
Your project’s rules: for example, use the tidyverse, build paths with here::here(), never setwd() or absolute paths
Ask for checks: have it print the numbers you will check against (next section)
The closing instructions: which .qmd and heading the code goes under, a sentence above each chunk, and render to HTML





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the file and look for itself. Still write down what you expect (number of rows, types of key columns) before it runs, so you have something to compare against.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Look at the file before you ask
text:
Look at the file before you ask

WhyRaw first lines of a csvCounting lines


You cannot describe a file you have not looked at, and you cannot check an import without knowing what the file holds. Two ways to look:

Open it: a csv in a text editor, an Excel file in Excel
Ask R to show the raw first lines, before any reader has guessed anything




readLines("corn_yields.csv", n = 3)

[1] "Year,State,FIPS,County_name,State_name,Commodity,Data item,Irrigated,Yield"                         
[2] "2008,31,31019,BUFFALO,NEBRASKA,CORN,\"CORN, GRAIN - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE\",0,173"           
[3] "2008,31,31019,BUFFALO,NEBRASKA,CORN,\"CORN, GRAIN, IRRIGATED - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE\",1,182"


From this you learn: the first line is column names, values are separated by commas, FIPS is a 5-digit code, one column name (Data item) has a space in it.



length(readLines("corn_yields.csv"))

[1] 162


162 lines, one of which is the column names. So a correct import has 161 rows. Write that number down before you import.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Read my corn data into R.
The AI has to guess the file name, its location, its format, its layout and what you want. A typical reply:

setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Documents")
corn <- read.csv("corn.csv")

It runs on nobody’s computer as written, and if you fix the path, it still guesses every type.


In my R project, the file data/corn_yields.xls is an Excel workbook with
two sheets, corn_yields_08 and corn_yields_09 (one per year). Each row is
one county, one year, and one irrigation status.

Write R code (tidyverse) that:
- reads BOTH sheets and stacks them into one table called corn
- keeps FIPS as text so leading zeros survive
- builds the path with here::here(), no setwd() and no absolute paths

Then print: the number of rows from each sheet (I expect 161 each), the
number of rows in corn (322), the type of every column, and the number
of missing values in each column.

Put the code in analysis/import.qmd under the heading "Read the corn
data", with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it
does and why. Render the document to HTML.


A version of what an AI returns for the strong request. Read it line by line; you should be able to say what each line does:

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)

path <- here::here("data", "corn_yields.xls")

corn_08 <- read_excel(path, sheet = "corn_yields_08", col_types = "text")
corn_09 <- read_excel(path, sheet = "corn_yields_09", col_types = "text")

corn <- bind_rows(corn_08, corn_09) |>
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year), Yield = as.numeric(Yield))

c(nrow(corn_08), nrow(corn_09), nrow(corn))
glimpse(corn)
colSums(is.na(corn))

bind_rows() stacks one table on top of another; you will meet it properly later in this chapter.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

The five checksAsking for themReading the HTML


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot decide which checks your file needs, and it cannot know the right answers. Ask for these after every import:










Ask the AI to print
Why
What only you can supply




1
the number of rows and columns
Rows go missing or appear when the wrong sheet is read or a title line is read as data
the row count from looking at the file


2
the type of every column
A wrong guess (an ID read as a number, a number read as text) gives no error
which type each key column should be


3
the number of missing values in each column
A missing-value code the reader was not told about, such as -999, is kept as a real value
how the file marks missing values


4
the smallest and largest value of each numeric column
Impossible values expose those codes, and unit mistakes
what range is believable


5
the first row
Shifted or merged columns show up at once
the same row in the raw file





One sentence at the end of your request does it:
After reading the file, print: the number of rows and columns, the type of
every column, the number of missing values in each column, the smallest and
largest value of each numeric column, and the first row.
Better still, tell it what you expect, so the HTML says which checks passed:
I expect 161 rows, 9 columns, no missing values, and Yield between 100 and
250. Print each check as "<check>: expected <X>, got <Y>".
The second version only works if you looked at the file first. That is the part you cannot hand off.


The AI writes the code. In the rendered HTML, you read what it printed and compare it with what you expected:


Code the AI wrote
list(
  rows_and_columns  = dim(corn),
  column_types      = sapply(corn, class),
  missing_per_column = colSums(is.na(corn)),
  yield_range       = range(corn$Yield)
)


$rows_and_columns
[1] 161   9

$column_types
       Year       State        FIPS County_name  State_name   Commodity 
  "numeric"   "numeric"   "numeric" "character" "character" "character" 
  Data item   Irrigated       Yield 
"character"   "numeric"   "numeric" 

$missing_per_column
       Year       State        FIPS County_name  State_name   Commodity 
          0           0           0           0           0           0 
  Data item   Irrigated       Yield 
          0           0           0 

$yield_range
[1] 103 204



161 rows: the file has 162 lines, one of them column names. Matches.
FIPS is a number. Fine here, since every Nebraska code starts with 31, but in a national dataset this is the column that loses leading zeros.
No missing values, and yields from 103 to 204 bushels per acre: believable.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The five checks apply to any file. The most useful checks come from what you know about this data, and no AI will think of them for you.
The two sheets of corn_yields.xls are labelled 2008 and 2009. Yields change from year to year, because the weather does. So ask:
Read both sheets of corn_yields.xls and tell me whether each county's
yield is the same in both years.


Code the AI wrote
yield_08 <- readxl::read_excel("corn_yields.xls", sheet = "corn_yields_08")
yield_09 <- readxl::read_excel("corn_yields.xls", sheet = "corn_yields_09")

identical(yield_08$Yield, yield_09$Yield)


[1] TRUE


TRUE: every county has exactly the same yield in both years. The code ran without error, and the row counts and types pass. The problem is in the file itself, and only a question based on what real yields look like found it.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “load corn_yields.xls and compute the average yield”, and got this:

setwd("C:/Users/jsmith/Desktop/class")
library(readxl)
corn <- read_excel("corn_yields.xls")
mean(corn$Yield)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each of the four lines do?
B. Which line will fail on your computer, and why?
C. Which problem would give a wrong answer without an error?
D. Rewrite the request so the AI could not make these mistakes.


A. Changes the working directory; loads readxl; reads the workbook into corn; averages the Yield column.
B. Line 1. The folder C:/Users/jsmith/... exists only on jsmith’s computer.
C. Line 3 reads only the first sheet, so the average covers 2008 only. Nothing says so.
D. Name both sheets, say whether you want both years or one, ask for here::here() and no setwd(), and ask it to print the row count per sheet.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What exporting is
text:
What exporting is
Exporting is importing in reverse: a function writes a table from R into a file. The line has the same parts, in the order object first, then path:

write_csv(corn, "corn_clean.csv")

The decision that is yours is the format, and it depends on who reads the file next and what has to survive:








Format
Choose it when
What is lost




csv
anyone, in any software, must be able to read it
every type: dates, factors and text IDs come back as guesses


rds
you, in R, will read it in the next step of the project
nothing, but only R can open it


dta
a collaborator uses STATA
some R-only types







A reasonable default


Keep raw data as you received it. Save intermediate results as rds, so types survive from one script to the next.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checking an export: the round trip
text:
Checking an export: the round trip
Why: a file can quietly keep less than you saved. The only way to know what it kept is to read it back.
What to ask: “Save the table, read it back, and compare it with the original.” Here Irrigated was first made a factor (a column of categories), then saved as csv and as rds:


Code the AI wrote
corn_f <- mutate(corn, Irrigated = factor(Irrigated, labels = c("no", "yes")))

csv_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn.csv")
rds_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn.rds")
write_csv(corn_f, csv_file)
saveRDS(corn_f, rds_file)

c(
  from_csv = class(read_csv(csv_file, show_col_types = FALSE)$Irrigated),
  from_rds = class(readRDS(rds_file)$Irrigated)
)


   from_csv    from_rds 
"character"    "factor" 


The csv gave back text: the factor was lost. The rds gave back the factor.




A full request


“Save corn as data/corn_clean.rds using here::here(), then read it back and tell me whether it matches the original exactly, and if not, which columns differ.”

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Requests you can copy
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you found by looking at the file. The blanks are the part the AI cannot fill in for you. Every request ends with the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsLook at a fileRead a csvRead an Excel workbookSave and read backExplain code


The lines that end every request:
Put the code in my Quarto document <analysis/ex-3-1.qmd>, under the
heading "<Task 2>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check as
"<check>: expected <X>, got <Y>". Render the document to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


Without reading <data/corn_messy.csv> as a table, show me its first
<5> raw lines and the total number of lines.

Put the code in my Quarto document <analysis/ex-3-1.qmd>, under the
heading "<Task 4b>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Render the document
to HTML.


In my R project, <data/corn_yields.csv> is a csv file. I looked at it:
- above the column names there is <nothing>
- there are <161> data rows and <9> columns
- one row is <one county, one year, one irrigation status>
- missing values are written as <nothing / -999 / .>
- ID columns that must stay text: <FIPS>
- a believable range for <Yield> is <100 to 250>

Read it into a table called <corn> using the tidyverse. Then check the
number of rows and columns, the type of every column, the number of
missing values in each column, the range of <Yield>, and the first row.

Put the code in my Quarto document <analysis/ex-3-1.qmd>, under the
heading "<Task 2>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check as
"<check>: expected <X>, got <Y>". Render the document to HTML.


In my R project, <data/corn_yields.xls> is an Excel workbook with the
sheets <corn_yields_08> and <corn_yields_09>. I want <both sheets,
stacked into one table called corn>. Each sheet has <161> rows, and
<Year> tells the sheets apart. ID columns that must stay text: <FIPS>.

Then check the number of rows from each sheet and in total, the type of
every column, the number of missing values in each column, and the
values of <Year>.

Put the code in my Quarto document <analysis/ex-3-1.qmd>, under the
heading "<Task 3>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check as
"<check>: expected <X>, got <Y>". Render the document to HTML.
